find: In your exam, examiners expect you to use meaningful names when writing programs or pseudo-code. Using single-letter variables (other than conventional loop counters like i) will cost marks on programming questions.
replace: The specification says you must use meaningful names when you write programs in the exam. A single-letter name, apart from a loop counter such as i, does not tell a reader what the variable is for.
note: F1: marks are awarded, never deducted; the 'will cost marks' claim is not in the specification

find: show that your name clearly describes the variable’s purpose — examiners will deduct marks for single-letter names except conventional loop counters.
replace: show that your name clearly describes the variable’s purpose — a single-letter name, apart from a loop counter, does not do that.
note: F1: GCSE mark schemes do not deduct marks

expect:

Developing: Example given without definition.
Emerging: Both same or neither appropriate.
value:

expect:
The following subroutine is intended to calculate and return the perimeter of a rectangle.

SUBROUTINE calcPerimeter(length, width)
   perimeter ← 2 + length + 2 + width
   RETURN perimeter
ENDSUBROUTINE

(a) Identify the error in the subroutine. [1 mark]
(b) Write a corrected version of the subroutine. [1 mark]
value:
The following subroutine is intended to calculate and return the perimeter of a rectangle.

SUBROUTINE calcPerimeter(length, width)
   perimeter ← 2 + length + 2 + width
   RETURN perimeter
ENDSUBROUTINE

(a) Identify the error in the subroutine. [1 mark]
(b) Write a corrected version of the subroutine. [3 marks]
note: F8: part (b) said 1 mark but the scheme awards 3, and the question is set at 4 marks

find:
Position / Character access — returns the character at a given index.
name[0] returns “L”. name[3] returns “d”.
replace:
Position — returns the index of the first place a character appears in a string.
POSITION(name, “n”) returns 2. Counting starts at 0, so “L” is index 0 and the first “n” is index 2.
note: F9: position returns an index for a character, not a character for an index

find:
Substring — extracts part of a string. The call is typically SUBSTRING(string, startIndex, length).
SUBSTRING(name, 1, 3) returns “ond”. (Start at index 1, take 3 characters.)
replace:
Substring — extracts part of a string. The call is SUBSTRING(startIndex, endIndex, string) and both index positions are included.
SUBSTRING(1, 3, name) returns “ond”. (The characters at index 1, 2 and 3.)
note: F10: AQA substring takes start index, end index, then the string; the third value is not a length

find: ASC(“A”) returns 65.
replace: CHAR_TO_CODE(“A”) returns 65.
note: F11: AQA pseudo-code names this operation CHAR_TO_CODE

find: CHR(65) returns “A”.
replace: CODE_TO_CHAR(65) returns “A”.
note: F11: AQA pseudo-code names this operation CODE_TO_CHAR

find: INT(“42”) returns the integer 42. STR(42) returns the string “42”.
replace: STRING_TO_INT(“42”) returns the integer 42. INT_TO_STRING(42) returns the string “42”.
note: F11: AQA pseudo-code names these STRING_TO_INT and INT_TO_STRING

find: Programs interact with users through INPUT and OUTPUT. The value from INPUT is always a string
replace: Programs interact with users through USERINPUT and OUTPUT. The value from USERINPUT is always a string
note: F12: AQA pseudo-code reads from the keyboard with USERINPUT

find: age ← INT(INPUT("Enter your age: "))
replace:
OUTPUT "Enter your age: "
age ← STRING_TO_INT(USERINPUT)
note: F12: INPUT() and INT() are not AQA pseudo-code

Complete the pseudo-code below by filling in the blank lines:

REPEAT
   age ← INT(INPUT("Enter your age: "))
UNTIL _____________________________

(a) Write the correct condition for the UNTIL line. [2 marks]
(b) State one example of erroneous test data for this routine, and explain what should happen. [2 marks]
